name: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (overview)
aliases: myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres

reference.source: ILAE classification / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A group of rare, mostly recessively inherited disorders defined by the combination of progressive myoclonus, other seizure types and neurological decline
Core features are action and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, generalised tonic-clonic seizures, progressive ataxia and cognitive decline
Important causes include Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease, the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, sialidoses and mitochondrial MERRF
Age at onset and the pace of decline help narrow the differential: Unverricht-Lundborg tends to be slowly progressive while Lafora disease progresses rapidly with prominent dementia
The EEG typically shows generalised epileptiform discharges with progressive background slowing and marked photosensitivity
Sodium-channel-blocking and some GABAergic agents can aggravate myoclonus, so drug choice must be considered carefully
Diagnosis increasingly relies on targeted genetic testing after clinical and electrophysiological characterisation
reference.pathophysiology: The progressive myoclonic epilepsies are a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders in which distinct molecular defects converge on progressive neuronal dysfunction and loss. Mechanisms include abnormal intracellular storage material (polyglucosan bodies in Lafora disease, lipopigment in the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses), impaired lysosomal enzyme function (sialidoses), defective protein handling (Unverricht-Lundborg disease) and mitochondrial energy failure (MERRF). These processes damage cortical, cerebellar and other networks, producing the characteristic cortical myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and cognitive deterioration that worsen over time.
additionalDifferentials: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and other genetic generalised epilepsies
Coeliac-related and other acquired myoclonus syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Targeted genetic and gene-panel testing after phenotyping
EEG demonstrating generalised discharges, background slowing and photosensitivity
Brain MRI, which may show cerebellar or generalised atrophy
Enzyme assays and tissue biopsy (e.g. skin, for characteristic inclusions) in selected disorders
Metabolic and mitochondrial studies including lactate and, where indicated, muscle biopsy
redFlags: Worsening action myoclonus with declining cognition rather than a stable course
Loss of ambulation from progressive ataxia and myoclonus
Seizure or myoclonus aggravation after introduction of an inappropriate antiseizure medication
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the specific disorder, ranging from a relatively slowly progressive course in Unverricht-Lundborg disease to relentless deterioration and early death in Lafora disease and some ceroid lipofuscinoses. Most forms cause increasing disability over years, and treatment is largely symptomatic.
pitfalls: Mislabelling early progressive myoclonic epilepsy as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and missing the progressive course
Using sodium-channel blockers or certain GABAergic agents that worsen myoclonus
Attributing progressive decline to poor seizure control rather than the underlying disease
Stopping the workup after clinical assessment without pursuing specific genetic or enzymatic diagnosis
